content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a framework called MONA for contrastive learning for image segmentation. The work combines aspects of the prior work by Tejankar et al. (2021) on iterative similarity distillation abbreviated ISD and that of Chaitanya et al (2020) combining local and global discrimination techniques. In addition it formulate contrastive losses called Tailness, Consistency, and Diversity to handled problems related to the claimed long-tailed class distribution of medical images, anatomical consistency, and diversity in sampled images. The approach is evaluated on three public medical imaging datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
---------
- The approach addresses the important and relevant problem of learning from limited labels in medical image segmentation.

- The approach is evaluated on three datasets showing good results in comparison to a quite large list of comparison approaches.

Weaknesses
----------
- Novelty is not very clearly described. Introduction contains almost a full page on the contributions of this paper, but it is relatively vague in pointing out how much of it is novel. A key innovation is mentioned, which is to paraphrase "seek diverse views (i.e., augmented/mined views) of different samples whose anatomical features are homogeneous within the same class type, while distinctive for different class types." I would argue that this is often the goal of contrastive learning in medical imaging depending on the definition of class, but perhaps I am misunderstanding why this is novel.

- More on novelty, the pre-training stage seems to be mostly derived from the referenced ISD (Tejankar et al. (2021) and Chaitanya et al. (2020). It is not clear to me if there are differences with these works or the novelty is mostly in the combination. I would suggest the authors consider how they present this to make it clear what their contribution is.

- Method appears to be 2D and the comparison approaches are also 2D including the fully supervised approach. The used datasets ACDC, LiTS, and MMWHS are all 3D and so I would assume 3D methods would work better in these cases. It could be acceptable to perform the comparison in 2D only, if the comparison was fair, the problem is however, that contrastive approaches may allow methods to more easily build a representation of the 3D anatomy. So a relevant question is, how much of the performance gains of these methods would still persists if models were working with 3D input.

- The selection of the reduced datasets seems unclear. How is the different percentages of labelled data selected? The datasets contain 20, 131, and 200 3D volumes respectively and you select 1 %, 5 % and 10 % of the labels in each of these? Is this by volume, by slice, labelled slice or?

- It is a paper presenting a framework, and at times it appears more like a sales pitch than science. I would suggest the authors rethink what the purpose of publishing works like this is. Personally I do not care that MONA is the best contrastive learning framework in the world, as it is not very beneficial to know. This is because frameworks will rarely be used as is and components will be replaced once improvements have been found or new will be added. To makes this worse, the code does not even appear to be available for download anywhere. One of the advantages of combining methods in a larger framework is the ability to study if the methods complement each other. Are the components merely achieving the same thing in different ways or do the benefits add up? The presented ablation study goes a little bit of the way to accomplish this, but I would have preferred if it was scaled up and been the main focus of the work.

- What is the computational requirements for training the proposed and investigated components? I think this is essential to document.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- I find the paper to be relatively hard to read and unclear. The grammar and spelling is fine, but the sentence structure and content appears to me to be unspecific and wordy.

- The quality of the work is low in my view as the authors are trying to do too much with too little. I find it hard to take much away from the work as there is so much going on and it appears confusing to me.

- Novelty is perhaps there, but I find it difficult to say with certainty.

- Reproducibility, no software or code is linked to and I do not find it likely that the work could be reproduced with high certainty.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work both proposes new components to the contrastive loss as well as including aspects that have been proposed before. As such it is a large and complicated framework that is difficult to describe, implement and evaluate convincingly within the page limits of conferences like ICLR. I would have much preferred a small clearly defined contribution that was evaluated clearly or even a combination of contrastive losses entirely from prior works that were evaluated fairly in a manner that would make the conclusions relevant for current usecases. This work I think wants to do too much and ends up just being confusing. I am not sure what to take away from it.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed a semi-supervised medical image segmentation method called Mine yOur owN Anatomy (MONA), aimming to solve a few performance issues at the semi-supervised learning of tailness, consistency and diversity. Authors gave descriptions on their understaind of these three terms/issues and proposed a few specialized loss functions to address them (as in section 3). Then three public medical image segmentation datasets: the ACDC dataset Bernard et al. (2018), the LiTS dataset Bilic et al. (2019), and the MMWHS dataset Zhuang & Shen (2016) are used for evaluation of the proposed method and comparison to a thorough list of other methods under 1%, 5
%, 10% labelled data setttings. Empirically favorable experimental results are reported.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ Three semi-supervised performance issues of tailness, consistency and diversity in designing medical image segmentation tasks are reasonable and relatively comprehensively discussed.
+ Authors read, summarize and derived several specialized loss functions that are targeted to address these three terms/issues. 
+ The overall technical framework is not very exciting but acceptable and reasonable as discussed above.

- The definition of these three terms are not new and may be discussed many times in previous work from a vast amount of literature. The precise description here is vague/ambiguous and not technically precise/sound. You kind of get the sense but still not very clear what exactly authors mean ... Auhtors really want to make their work look significant but I am not sure if they achieve that goal. These three terms (tailness, etc.) may be more obvious in medical diagnosis and medical image recogniton, instead of pixel-levels for the segmentation problem. If you look at the figure on Page 5, not sure why distinguishing these sparse points will improve segmentation which is a structured dense prediction problem.

- In the technical section, author did a good work on reviewing previous work, but it is unclear what loss functions are completely novel and what are somehow derived from previous work in section 3. Judging the novelty and technical significance of the proposed loss functions is not straightforward.

- The experimental results on using 10% labels to beat the fully supervised setting are little exciting. I would assume that the proposed method really select well these 10% labelled data instances but there is no explicit experiments to support such. There is no much detailed description on the segmentation network architectures that are used. From these analytical loss functions, almost suddently, you will see so many numbers to demonstrate the superior performance here and there. No adequate description details on addressing the reproducibility issues of this paper.

- These three datasets are relatively easy/popular/well-studied medical imaging segmentation problems. Authors did not actually solve any segmentation problems that can not be solved well before.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework termed Mine yOur owN Anatomy (MONA) based on different anatomical views. The method consists of two steps: (1) semi-supervised pre-training, and (2) anatomical contrastive reconstruction fine-tuning. They evaluated the performance on three public medical image segmentation datasets with different labeled settings to validate the effectiveness of MONA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

-- Authors consider and analyze three pitfalls of contrastive learning in medical segmentation: tailness, consistency, and diversity.

-- In the CL framework, authors show two simple solutions towards learning invariances – through the use of stronger data augmentations and nearest neighbors. Moreover, they construct a set of objectives that encourage the model to be capable of decomposing medical images into a collection of anatomical features in an unsupervised manner.

-- On the own split training/testing set, authors show MONA's performance is in general superior to many other semi-supervised methods.


Weakness: 

-- The novelty of this method is moderate. The method consists of two steps: (1) semi-supervised pre-training, and (2) anatomical contrastive reconstruction fine-tuning. Step (1) is built upon ISD (Tejankar et al. 2021)  and global and local instance discrimination strategies is adopted similarly of Chaitanya et al. (2020).

-- The experimental evaluation is not sufficiently convincing. (1) Authors has used the 3 public datasets. However, they did not report the results on the official testing dataset, e.g. they train and evaluated using the 131 CT scans provided by the organizer as training/validation instead of reporting the results on the official 70 testing scans. Reporting the results on the testing set would not only be more convincing, but also have a fair comparison to the fully-supervised methods' performance (since authors claim that MONA exceeds the fully supervised methods when using 10% labeled data). (2) The fully supervised counterparts' performance may not be convincing. E.g., it is a basic 2D UNet structure instead of 3D (3D network normally has better segmentation performance in medical imaging especially for tumors). This supervised model cannot be treated as leading supervised segmentation methods, e.g, nnUNet.

-- Some demonstrations seem not meaningful and have error. E.g. Fig 1 shows examples of three benchmarks (i.e., ACDC, LiTS, MMWHS) with large intra-class variances. However, it is hardly to see what are the intra-class variances in the three 2D images.

-- Some of the statements may not be valid. E.g., (1) in section Anatomical Contrastive Reconstruction, "The high-level idea is that the features should be very similar among the same class type, while very dissimilar across different class types.". This might not be true for medical images, where it often exhibits large intra-class variation for the same class type. (2) at the 4th paragraph of the Introduction, "Considering performing pixel-level CL with medical images is impractical for both memory cost and training time". This may not be true. "Self-supervised learning of pixel-wise anatomical embeddings in radiological images, TMI 2021" which is a pixel wise CL work in medical images.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity and quality of this work is satisfactory. The novelty is moderate. The reproducibility seems OK.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please see the detailed comments above. The paper has some merits, but also have quite a few major concerns. I reviewed this paper in another conference. It is unfortunate that authors have completely ignored my previous concerns.

content.title: Mine yOur owN Anatomy: Revisiting Medical Image Segmentation with Extremely Limited Labels
content.TL;DR: This paper proposes a semi-supervised contrastive learning framework that seamlessly assembles three effective principles: tailness, consistency, and diversity, which outperforms existing semi-supervised and fully-supervised competitors.
content.abstract: Recent studies on contrastive learning have achieved remarkable performance solely by leveraging few labels in the context of medical image segmentation. Existing methods mainly focus on instance discrimination and invariant mapping (i.e., pulling positive samples closer and negative samples apart in the feature space). However, they face three common pitfalls: (1) tailness: medical image data usually follows an implicit long-tail class distribution. Blindly leveraging all pixels in training hence can lead to the data imbalance issues, and cause deteriorated performance; (2) consistency: it remains unclear whether a segmentation model has learned meaningful and yet consistent anatomical features due to the intra-class variations between different anatomical features; and (3) diversity: the intra-slice correlations within the entire dataset have received significantly less attention. This motivates us to seek a principled approach for strategically making use of the dataset itself to discover similar yet distinct samples from different anatomical views. In this paper, we introduce a novel semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework termed Mine yOur owN Anatomy (MONA), and make three contributions. First, prior work argues that every pixel equally matters to the model training; we observe empirically that this alone is unlikely to define meaningful anatomical features, mainly due to lacking the supervision signal. We show two simple solutions towards learning invariances -- through the use of stronger data augmentations and nearest neighbors. Second, we construct a set of objectives that encourage the model to be capable of decomposing medical images into a collection of anatomical features in an unsupervised manner. Lastly, our extensive results on three benchmark datasets with different labeled settings validate the effectiveness of our proposed MONA which achieves new state-of-the-art under different labeled settings. Perhaps most impressively, MONA trained with 10% labeled -- for the first time -- outperforms the supervised counterpart on all three datasets. MONA makes minimal assumptions on domain expertise, and hence constitutes a practical and versatile solution in medical image analysis. Codes will be made available to the public.
